summary.case_overview: This judgment of a 13-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (Writ Petition (Civil) 135 of 1970, decided on 24/04/1973) deals with constitutional writ petitions challenging the validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments to the Constitution of India [Page 1] [Page 2]. The primary legal question before the Court was to determine the true scope and extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, specifically whether there are inherent or implied limitations that prevent Parliament from abrogating fundamental rights or altering the basic structure or framework of the Constitution, and whether I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correctly decided [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 309] [Page 488] [Page 501]. The Court held that while Parliament possesses broad constituent powers to amend any provision of the Constitution under Article 368, that amending power does not extend to destroying or damaging the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501].
summary.facts_of_case: Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 was filed on March 21, 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution by His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru for enforcement of his fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31 [Page 1]. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964) as amended by the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 (Act 35 of 1969) [Page 1]. During the pendency of the writ petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act 25 of 1971) was enacted and received Presidential assent on August 7, 1971 [Page 1]. Subsequently, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act (in force from November 5, 1971), the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act (in force from April 20, 1972), and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act (in force from June 9, 1972) [Page 2]. The Twenty-ninth Amendment inserted Kerala Acts 35 of 1969 and 25 of 1971 into the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution [Page 2]. The Supreme Court granted leave on August 10, 1972 to amend the petition and urge additional grounds challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments [Page 1] [Page 2]. The matter was referred to a larger bench of 13 Judges to determine the validity of the impugned constitutional amendments and reconsider the correctness of the decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab [Page 2] [Page 6].
summary.legal_issues:
1. Whether the decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correctly decided in holding that Parliament has no power to amend Part III of the Constitution so as to take away or abridge fundamental rights and that the amending power is derived from ordinary legislative entries [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 309] [Page 501].
2. What is the true extent, scope, and ambit of the power conferred on Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368 [Page 2] [Page 78] [Page 104] [Page 309] [Page 485].
3. Whether there are inherent or implied limitations on the amending power of Parliament under Article 368 preventing it from altering, damaging, or destroying the basic structure, essential features, or identity of the Constitution [Page 6] [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 488].
4. Whether the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 6] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 494].
5. Whether Section 2 and Section 3 (introducing Article 31C) of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 are constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 194] [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 374] [Page 495] [Page 498].
6. Whether the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is constitutionally valid [Page 2] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500].
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
Petitioners' Submissions:
- Counsel for the petitioners argued that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is limited and does not empower Parliament to alter or destroy the essential features, basic structure, or identity of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 78] [Page 91] [Page 258] [Page 488].
- It was contended that fundamental rights enshrined in Part III represent essential human freedoms and natural rights that were intended to be permanent and beyond the reach of parliamentary majorities [Page 2] [Page 181] [Page 487] [Page 488].
- It was submitted that 'law' in Article 13(2) includes constitutional amendments, and therefore any amendment taking away or abridging fundamental rights is void [Page 3] [Page 117] [Page 485].
- Regarding Article 31C, the petitioners submitted that it subverts the supremacy of the Constitution, delegates amending power to State Legislatures, abrogates essential fundamental rights, and excludes judicial review through its declaration clause [Page 2] [Page 245] [Page 496] [Page 499].

Respondents' Submissions:
- Counsel for the respondents submitted that Article 368 confers an unlimited, plenary, and sovereign amending power on Parliament that extends to every part and provision of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 104] [Page 271] [Page 488].
- It was argued that there are no express, inherent, or implied limitations on the amending power, and Parliament can alter any feature, including fundamental rights, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, or even democratic form of government [Page 2] [Page 104] [Page 181] [Page 271] [Page 488].
- It was contended that 'law' in Article 13(2) applies only to ordinary statutory laws enacted under legislative powers and does not apply to constitutional amendments passed under constituent power [Page 3] [Page 117] [Page 485] [Page 486].
- Respondents submitted that socio-economic objectives in Directive Principles (Part IV), such as Article 39(b) and (c), require wide amending powers to remove inequalities and redistribute community resources [Page 104] [Page 194] [Page 284] [Page 497].
summary.court_reasoning:
1. Correctness of Golak Nath: The Court reasoned that Article 368 is not merely a procedural provision but contains the substantive constituent power as well as procedure to amend the Constitution [Page 6] [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 484] [Page 501]. The word 'law' in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary legislative enactments and does not apply to constitutional amendments made in exercise of constituent power under Article 368 [Page 3] [Page 117] [Page 129] [Page 485] [Page 486] [Page 501].
2. Basic Structure Doctrine: Sikri, C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Jaganmohan Reddy, and Khanna, JJ. held that the word 'amendment' in Article 368 implies retention of the general identity and basic framework of the Constitution; it does not comprehend the power to alter, emasculate, destroy, or abrogate the essential features or basic structure of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 104] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 309] [Page 374]. Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, and Chandrachud, JJ. reasoned that Article 368 confers broad constituent power reaching every provision without implied or inherent limitations [Page 155] [Page 181] [Page 271] [Page 451] [Page 484] [Page 488] [Page 501].
3. Twenty-fourth Amendment: The Court held that the 24th Amendment is valid as it merely clarified the pre-existing legal position that Article 368 contains constituent power to amend any provision and that Article 13(2) does not restrict amendments [Page 6] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 484] [Page 494] [Page 501].
4. Twenty-fifth Amendment (Section 2 - Article 31(2)): The Court reasoned that substituting the word 'amount' for 'compensation' eliminates the requirement of paying full market value or 'just equivalent' for acquired property; however, the amount fixed or principles laid down must not be illusory or arbitrary [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 497] [Page 498] [Page 501].
5. Twenty-fifth Amendment (Section 3 - Article 31C): The majority of Judges held that the first part of Article 31C protecting laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31 is valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 498] [Page 501]. However, the second part of Article 31C containing the declaration clause ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court...') was held invalid and severable because it sought to completely exclude judicial review, which is an essential feature [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 425] [Page 501].
6. Twenty-ninth Amendment: The Court reasoned that placing statutory enactments in the Ninth Schedule provides protection under Article 31B and does not violate constituent power [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
1. Overruled I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, holding that Article 368 contains both the power and procedure for constitutional amendment, and that 'law' in Article 13(2) does not extend to constitutional amendments [Page 6] [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 501].
2. Declared that Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501].
3. Upheld the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 494] [Page 501].
4. Upheld Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, subject to the finding that the 'amount' fixed or determined for compulsory acquisition must not be illusory [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 497] [Page 501].
5. Upheld the first part of Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 (introducing Article 31C), but declared the second part of Article 31C containing the finality/declaration clause ('and no law containing a declaration...') invalid and severed it [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501].
6. Upheld the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501].
7. Remitted the writ petitions to the Constitution Bench for final disposal in accordance with law [Page 374] [Page 502].

summary.simplified_explanation: In simple terms, this judgment examined whether Parliament has unrestricted power to change the Indian Constitution. The Supreme Court established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine', ruling that while Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368—including fundamental rights—it cannot change, destroy, or alter the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501]. The Court reversed its previous decision in the Golak Nath case, clarifying that constitutional amendments are made under constituent power and are not ordinary laws restricted by Article 13(2) [Page 6] [Page 129] [Page 486] [Page 501]. The Court upheld the 24th and 29th Amendments [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 501]. Regarding the 25th Amendment, it permitted replacing the word 'compensation' with 'amount' for acquired property as long as the amount is not illusory [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 497] [Page 501]. However, the Court struck down the portion of Article 31C that tried to prevent courts from evaluating whether a law actually fulfilled socio-economic goals, preserving judicial review [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 498] [Page 501].
